items.question: Why is Shiva described as unfixed, all-pervading, eternal, and universal in form?
premises: Shiva is not fixed or limited.
He is all-pervading and therefore present everywhere.
He is eternal and therefore without beginning or end.
He has the form of the universe.
items.inference: Because Shiva is all-pervading, eternal, and universal in form, he is not subject to limitation in space, time, or shape.
items.plain_english: Shiva is not fixed or limited. He is all-pervading and eternal, and he takes the form of the whole universe. Because he pervades everything, he is present everywhere; because he is eternal, he has no beginning or end.

items.question: Why is Shiva said to have manifold forms in the scriptures?
premises: Shiva has the universe as his form.
As such, he manifests the variety of conscious and unconscious things.
Scriptures like the Dikshottara state his manifold formhood.
items.inference: Shiva is described as manifold because his universal form appears as the diverse conscious and unconscious world.
items.plain_english: Because Shiva takes the universe as his form, he appears as the full variety of conscious and unconscious things. For this reason, texts such as the Dikshottara say that he has many forms.

items.question: In what sixfold way is Shiva said to be expressed?
premises: Shiva is identified with world, body, light, space, sound, and mantra.
The mantra aspect includes bindu, nada, and related forms.
This gives a sixfold description of Shiva.
items.inference: Shiva is spoken of in six modes that range from cosmic and bodily forms to subtle sonic and mantric forms.
items.plain_english: Shiva is said to appear in six ways: as the world, as a body, as light, as space, as sound, and as mantra. The mantric form also includes bindu, nada, and related expressions.

items.question: How does knowledge of space, sound, and related forms lead to liberation?
premises: One who is established in a particular nature attains that state.
Space, sound, and related forms are modes of Shiva.
Knowledge of these modes leads to the supreme state.
items.inference: By becoming established in the knowledge of Shiva's sonic and spatial forms, one attains supreme liberation.
items.plain_english: Whoever becomes firmly established in a particular nature comes to share in that state. Since space, sound, and related forms are ways Shiva appears, true knowledge of them leads to supreme liberation without doubt.

items.question: What does the Lord's universal form indicate about limitation and unlimitedness?
premises: The Lord has the universe as his form.
This universal form is only an indicative mark, not a final boundary.
In him, limitation dissolves within unlimitedness.
items.inference: The Lord's universal form points to a reality in which all apparent limits are absorbed into his unlimited nature.
items.plain_english: The Lord's having the universe as his form is only an indication of his nature. Even when he appears in limited forms, those limits dissolve within his unlimited being.

items.question: How does the Kamika describe the Lord's pervasion of all things?
premises: The Kamika states that the Lord is both of all forms and formless.
He pervades all moving and unmoving things.
The image of water and a mirror illustrates this pervasive presence.
items.inference: The Lord pervades the entire universe while remaining both manifest in all forms and beyond form.
items.plain_english: The Kamika says that the Lord has all forms and yet is also formless. Like water or a mirror, he pervades everything, both moving and unmoving.

items.question: Are Shiva's qualities such as pervasion really separate from one another?
premises: Qualities like pervasion are attributed to Shiva.
These qualities are not mutually divided in him.
They function as one quality that includes all.
items.inference: Shiva's many attributed qualities are expressions of a single all-inclusive reality.
uncertainties: The exact first member of vimutādyaḥ is slightly compressed in the transmitted form.
items.plain_english: Qualities such as pervasion and the rest are not really separate in Shiva. They are not divided from one another, but operate as one single quality that includes everything.

items.question: How can Shiva be said to have many powers without losing unity?
premises: Shiva is endowed with the power of freedom.
He is also spoken of as having many powers.
These many powers are not separate from that one power.
items.inference: Shiva's many powers are expressions of his one power of freedom and do not compromise his unity.
items.plain_english: So the straightforward conclusion is that Shiva is endowed with the power of freedom. Even when he is said to have many powers, those powers are not separate from that one power.

items.question: What is meant by calling Shiva both nondual and a possessor of power?
premises: Power is the own form of a being as projected by the knowing subject.
Shiva is nondual in reality.
He can still be conceived as possessing power.
items.inference: The attribution of power to Shiva does not create real duality, because power is his own form as it appears in cognition.
items.plain_english: Power is simply a being's own form as it is projected by the knowing subject. For that reason, Shiva remains nondual even when he is thought of as possessing power.

items.question: Is there any real difference among the Lord's various projected forms?
premises: The Lord's various bodies are projected by the knowing subject.
A single reality can appear with different functions.
Fire remains one while burning and cooking.
items.inference: There is no real difference among the Lord's various forms, only different appearances of one reality.
items.plain_english: When the Lord appears in different bodies as projected by the knowing subject, there is no real difference between them. It is like fire, which remains one whether it is burning or cooking.

items.question: Is there anything real in Shiva apart from manifestation or a real split between power and possessor?
premises: In ultimate truth, Shiva is nothing apart from manifestation.
Power and possessor of power are distinguished conceptually.
No real difference exists between them.
items.inference: Ultimately, Shiva is pure manifestation, and the distinction between power and possessor is not ultimately real.
items.plain_english: In the highest sense, Shiva is nothing other than manifestation itself. There is no real thing apart from that shining, and there is no ultimately real difference between his power and the one who possesses it.

items.question: How can the Goddess appear as other while still being identical with the one reality?
premises: Whatever produces the surge of a reality's own power is identical with that reality.
Such a power is still called power.
The Goddess can appear with another form while remaining that same reality.
items.inference: The Goddess is the one reality's own power, appearing as other without being ultimately different from it.
items.plain_english: Whatever brings forth the surge of a reality's own power is not different from that reality, because it is identical with it. That is power, and in this way the Goddess appears with another form even while remaining the same reality.
